english: Excuse me, but… / Sorry to bother you, but… (polite lead-in before asking a stranger something)
usage: Excuse me, but may I ask you for directions?
Classic opener to a stranger on the street
Excuse me, but may I have your name?
Softens a personal question; very polite
Excuse me, is this seat taken?
Approaching someone in a cafe or on the subway
Sorry to bother you, do you have a moment?
Before stopping someone who looks busy
examples: 실례지만, 이 근처에 약국이 어디 있어요?
Excuse me, but where's a pharmacy around here?
Asking a passerby
실례지만, 혹시 한국분이세요?
Excuse me, but are you Korean by any chance?
혹시 doubles the politeness/hedging
실례지만 먼저 좀 지나가도 될까요?
Sorry, but may I get past you?
Squeezing past in a crowded place
nuance: Polite/formal lead-in (존댓말) used right before you impose on a stranger or ask something slightly personal. It signals 'I know I'm interrupting you.' With people you know well it sounds too stiff; among friends you'd just say 저기 or 미안한데.
mistakes: Don't confuse it with 실례합니다 (a standalone 'excuse me' to get attention). 실례지만 must be followed by your actual request — it can't stand alone.

english: The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)
usage: The thing is, I have a favor to ask.
다름이 아니라 잠깐 드릴 말씀이 있어서요.
Actually, there's something I wanted to tell you.
다름이 아니라, 다음 주 일정 때문에 연락드렸어요.
I'm reaching out about next week's schedule, actually.
Stating the purpose of a call/email
다름이 아니고 돈 좀 빌릴 수 있을까 해서.
So, the thing is, I was wondering if I could borrow some money.
examples: 여보세요? 다름이 아니라 예약 변경 좀 하려고 전화드렸어요.
Hello? The thing is, I'm calling to change my reservation.
Phone opener after the greeting
다름이 아니라 혹시 이번 주말에 시간 되세요?
So, the reason I ask is — are you free this weekend by any chance?
Building up to an invitation
과장님, 다름이 아니라 연차 하루만 쓸 수 있을까요?
Manager, the thing is, could I take just one day of leave?
Polite workplace request
nuance: Polite spoken/written set phrase that buys a second before you reveal why you really called or approached someone. It frames what follows as 'the actual matter,' so the listener braces for a request or announcement. Common in phone calls, emails, and talking to seniors; 다름이 아니고 is the looser conversational form.
mistakes: It's a lead-in, not a full sentence — always attach your actual point after it.
Spelling: 다름이 (not 다림이). It comes from 다르다 (to differ).

english: Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)
usage: 죄송한데 조금만 조용히 해 주실 수 있어요?
Sorry, but could you keep it down a little?
죄송한데 = slightly shorter; asking a stranger
죄송한데요, 지금은 좀 어려울 것 같아요.
I'm sorry, but it'd be hard right now.
Excuse me, could you let me through?
examples: 죄송한데요, 주문한 거랑 다른 게 나왔어요.
Sorry, but this isn't what I ordered.
Flagging a mistake at a restaurant, politely
죄송한데 혹시 자리 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있을까요?
Sorry, but could we possibly switch seats?
On a train/plane
죄송한데요, 제가 지금 통화가 좀 어려워서요.
I'm sorry, but I can't really talk right now.
Trailing -서요 leaves it gently unfinished
nuance: Polite (존댓말) cushion that opens with an apology, so it feels softer and more deferential than 실례지만. Koreans reach for it constantly when complaining, refusing, or asking a small favor, because leading with 죄송 keeps things smooth. 죄송한데 (no 요) is the same in casual-polite speech.
mistakes: Don't write 죄성한데요 — it's 죄송 (罪悚).
It's not a real apology for wrongdoing; if you actually did something wrong, use 죄송합니다 properly, not just this softener.

english: Yeah, right? / I know, tell me about it / You're so right (agreeing, often with a sigh)
usage: I know, right? Why's it so hot these days?
Agreeing and adding to the complaint
그러게 = casual; 내 말이 reinforces agreement
Yeah… we really should've booked earlier.
Agreeing with a tinge of regret
examples: A: 차가 진짜 막히네요. B: 그러게요.
A: Traffic's really bad. B: Yeah, I know.
Resigned agreement
A: 물가가 너무 올랐어요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 장 보기 무서워요.
A: Prices have gone up so much. B: Tell me about it, I'm scared to grocery shop.
Empathetic agreement + add-on
A: 그 사람 좀 이상하지 않아요? B: 그러게요, 저도 그렇게 느꼈어요.
A: Isn't that person a bit odd? B: Right? I felt the same.
Confirming a shared impression
nuance: Conversational agreement that means 'I feel the same, you're right' — usually said with empathy or a shared sigh, not just neutral 'yes.' It often implies you've been thinking the same thing. 그러게요 is casual-polite; 그러게 / 그러게 말이야 among close friends.
mistakes: It's not a question — don't use it to ask 'why?'.
Avoid using it to agree with praise about yourself; it's for agreeing with the other person's observation, not accepting a compliment.

english: It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)
usage: Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped.
Can't be helped — let's go next time.
If it's sold out, oh well, nothing to do.
Trailing 뭐 adds a resigned shrug
I had no choice but to take a taxi.
어쩔 수 없이 = 'unavoidably' as an adverb
examples: A: 기차표가 다 매진이에요. B: 그래요? 어쩔 수 없죠.
A: The train tickets are all sold out. B: Oh well, can't be helped.
Graceful resignation
오늘 약속 취소됐는데, 어쩔 수 없죠 뭐.
Today's plan got canceled, but oh well, what can you do.
Letting it go
몸이 안 좋으면 쉬어야죠, 어쩔 수 없어요.
If you're not well you have to rest — there's no other way.
어쩔 수 없어요 = flatter, plain statement
nuance: Casual-polite phrase for gracefully accepting something you can't change — a verbal shrug. The -죠 ending makes it feel like 'well, that's just how it is, right?' Said calmly it signals acceptance; said sharply it can sound passive-aggressive ('fine, whatever'), so tone matters.
mistakes: Don't use it about things you actually can control — it implies the situation is genuinely out of your hands.
어쩔 수 없죠 (accepting) vs 어쩔 수 없이 (the adverb 'unavoidably') are different forms; don't swap them.

english: Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)
usage: Not at all, of course I should help.
Please, I'm the one who's grateful.
무슨 말씀을 (no 요) = slightly shorter, still polite
Oh come on, don't say that.
What do you mean — you're not late at all.
무슨 말씀이세요 = 'what are you saying?' to gently contradict
examples: A: 정말 감사합니다. B: 무슨 말씀을요, 별거 아니에요.
A: Thank you so much. B: Oh, don't mention it, it was nothing.
Polite response to thanks
A: 음식 솜씨가 정말 좋으시네요. B: 무슨 말씀을요.
A: You're such a great cook. B: Oh, you're too kind.
Humbly deflecting a compliment
A: 폐 끼쳐서 죄송해요. B: 무슨 말씀을요, 괜찮아요.
A: Sorry for being a bother. B: Not at all, it's fine.
Reassuring after an apology
nuance: Polite, humble phrase (uses honorific 말씀) for waving away thanks, praise, or an apology — literally 'what words [are you saying]!' It's warmer and more deferential than a flat 아니에요 and very common with elders, customers, or anyone you're being courteous to. The full form is 무슨 말씀을 (하세요).
mistakes: Use 말씀 (honorific), not 말 — 무슨 말을요 sounds off here.
It deflects, so don't follow it by then accepting the praise; pair it with a modest add-on like 별거 아니에요.

english: Don't worry about it / Don't trouble yourself / Never mind it (telling someone to let something go)
usage: I'm fine, so please don't worry about it.
Don't worry about stuff like that.
신경 쓰지 마 = casual, to a friend
제 건 신경 쓰지 마시고 먼저 드세요.
Don't bother about mine — go ahead and eat first.
Telling a host not to fuss over you
남들 말 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요.
Don't pay so much attention to what others say.
Comforting someone who's stressed by gossip
examples: A: 자리까지 안 치워서 죄송해요. B: 신경 쓰지 마세요, 제가 할게요.
A: Sorry I didn't clear the table. B: Don't worry about it, I'll do it.
Putting someone at ease
바쁘실 텐데 제 일은 신경 쓰지 마세요.
You must be busy — please don't trouble yourself over my matter.
Polite at work
사소한 일이니까 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요.
It's a trivial thing, so don't dwell on it.
Reassuring
nuance: Polite-casual phrase meaning 'don't expend mental energy on this' (신경 = nerves/attention, 쓰다 = to use). It reassures someone who feels bad, is fussing over you, or is anxious about others' opinions. 신경 쓰지 마 for friends; 신경 쓰지 마세요 / 마시고 for polite contexts.
mistakes: Don't write 신경쓰지 as one word in careful writing — standard spacing is 신경 쓰지.
To a senior, the bare imperative can feel curt; soften with 너무 ('don't worry too much') or pair with 괜찮아요.

english: Pretty much / More or less, yeah / You could say that (loosely confirming something as roughly true)
usage: 그런 셈 치다 = 'let's regard it as so', casual
examples: A: 그럼 두 분이 사귀는 거예요? B: 뭐… 그런 셈이죠.
A: So you two are dating? B: Well… more or less, yeah.
Half-admitting with a smile
A: 이제 한국 생활에 적응한 거네요? B: 네, 그런 셈이죠.
A: So you've adjusted to life in Korea now? B: Yeah, pretty much.
Approximate agreement
하루 종일 일했으니 쉰 날이 없는 셈이에요.
I worked all day, so it's basically like I had no day off.
셈이다 expressing 'it amounts to'
nuance: Casual-polite phrase for confirming something as approximately true when it's not 100% exact — 'in effect, that's the case.' The -죠 ending invites soft agreement. 셈 means 'reckoning/count,' so X인 셈이다 = 'it counts as X.' Great for vague yes-answers without overcommitting.
mistakes: For a firm, exact 'yes,' use 맞아요 — 그런 셈이죠 always carries an 'approximately' nuance.
Don't mix up 셈 (reckoning) with 샘 (spring/jealousy); the phrase is 그런 셈.

english: That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)
usage: 음… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같은데요.
Umm… that might be a little difficult.
Left unfinished on purpose — the 'no' is implied
That's kind of… not great, don't you think?
그건 좀 그렇다 = 'that's kind of iffy'
Same trailing pattern with any noun + 좀
examples: A: 오늘 밤에 시간 돼요? B: 아, 오늘은 좀….
A: Are you free tonight? B: Ah, tonight is a bit…
Declining an invite without a hard 'no'
A: 이 색깔 어때요? B: 음, 그건 좀….
A: How about this color? B: Hmm, that's kind of…
Softly expressing dislike
같이 투자하자는 건 좀… 죄송해요.
Investing together is a bit… sorry.
Politely refusing a proposal
nuance: Very Korean indirect refusal: you trail off after 좀 ('a little') and let silence carry the 'no.' Saying the rest out loud would feel too blunt, so the unfinished sentence is the polite point. Works in both casual and polite speech; tone and a small grimace do the work.
mistakes: Don't finish it bluntly with 싫어요 ('I don't like it') — that defeats the soft purpose.
Foreign learners often miss this as a refusal and keep pushing; in Korea, 그건 좀… usually means no.

english: No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')
usage: 말도 안 돼, 그게 어떻게 가능해?
That's absurd — how is that even possible?
말도 안 되는 소리 하지 마.
examples: A: 그 식당 한 시간 기다려야 한대요. B: 한 시간이요? 말도 안 돼요!
A: They say you wait an hour for that place. B: An hour? That's ridiculous!
Indignant disbelief
복권 당첨됐다고? 말도 안 돼!
You won the lottery? No way!
Excited shock with friends
이 월세에 이 방은 말도 안 돼요.
This room for this rent makes no sense.
Judging something unreasonable
nuance: High-emotion exclamation literally meaning 'it doesn't even become words' — i.e., it's so absurd/shocking it can't be reasoned. Used for happy shock, indignation, or 'that's nonsense.' 말도 안 돼 with friends, 말도 안 돼요 in polite speech. Context and tone decide whether it's delighted or angry.
mistakes: Spacing: 말도 안 돼요 (안 is separate). 돼요 not 되요.
Don't aim it at a person's character ('you're ridiculous'); it targets a statement or situation, not the person.

english: I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)
usage: 그럴 줄 알았어, 네가 또 늦을 줄.
I knew it — that you'd be late again.
I knew it would turn out like this.
examples: A: 그 가게 망했대요. B: 그럴 줄 알았어요, 손님이 없더라고요.
A: That shop went under. B: I figured — there were never any customers.
Confirming a prediction
A: 시험 또 떨어졌어. B: 놀자고 할 때 알아봤어, 그럴 줄 알았어.
A: I failed the exam again. B: I could tell when you wanted to hang out — I knew it.
Mild 'told you so' to a friend
역시 비가 오네, 그럴 줄 알았어.
Of course it's raining — I had a feeling.
역시 ('as expected') reinforces it
nuance: Casual-polite phrase for 'this is exactly what I predicted.' It can sound knowing/sympathetic or like a smug 'told you so' depending on tone — be careful using it when someone just had bad luck. The pattern is V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알았다 ('I knew/expected that ~').
mistakes: 줄 here means 'fact/way,' unrelated to 줄 'a line/rope' — don't translate literally.
After someone's misfortune, a flat 그럴 줄 알았어 can feel rude; add empathy or soften it.

english: No pressure / Don't feel obligated / Please don't feel burdened (about a gift, favor, or invitation)
usage: 그냥 작은 선물이니까 부담 갖지 마세요.
It's just a small gift, so please don't feel burdened.
Don't stress about it, just come comfortably.
부담 갖지 말고 = casual, inviting a friend
If it feels like too much, you don't have to.
I'm not trying to pressure you.
examples: A: 이렇게 비싼 걸 어떻게 받아요. B: 부담 갖지 마세요, 제 마음이에요.
A: How can I accept something this expensive? B: No pressure, it's just my way of showing I care.
Easing a gift recipient
식사 한번 대접하고 싶어서요. 부담 갖지 마시고 시간 되실 때 오세요.
I'd like to treat you to a meal. No pressure — just come whenever you're free.
Polite invitation
거절해도 괜찮으니까 부담 갖지 마세요.
It's totally fine to say no, so don't feel obligated.
Lowering the pressure of a request
nuance: Polite-casual phrase that releases the other person from a sense of obligation (부담 = burden/pressure). Koreans say it constantly when giving gifts, extending invitations, or asking favors, because accepting can feel like incurring a debt. 부담 갖지 마세요 in polite speech; 부담 갖지 마 with friends.
mistakes: The verb is 갖다 (to have/hold) → 부담 갖지 마세요, literally 'don't hold the burden.'
Don't overuse it to the point of insisting; saying it once warmly is enough — repeating it can ironically add pressure.
